articles.title: 🌿 NatureLens: Turning Screen Time into Green Time
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass. NatureLens is a nature companion designed to help people step away from their screens and reconnect with the wo…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass . What I Built NatureLens is a nature companion designed to help people step away from their screens and reconnect with the world around them. 🌱 In a world where we spend hours scrolling, I wanted to build something that uses technology to encourage people to spend more time outdoors—not less. NatureLens turns going outside into a simple, engaging experience through nature-focused activities and exploration. The idea is simple: instead of spending more time consuming content on a screen, use the screen as a starting point for discovering something in the real world. NatureLens is designed for students, nature lovers, and anyone who wants to build a healthier relationship with technology.

articles.body: For the Touch Grass theme I built something that makes the screen the shortest part of the experience: a stargazing guide for Bengaluru terraces that tells you what's actually above the horizon right now — then sends you outside. What I built Terrace Sky Spotter — a web app (vanilla HTML/JS + zero-dependency Python server, stdlib only) in two halves: Deterministic astronomy (code, not AI): 16 anchor stars from open catalogs (Yale Bright Star Catalogue / HYG, public domain) + real Julian-date → sidereal-time math computes altitude/azimuth for 12.97°N 77.59°E. No GPS, no network. Tap any constellation for its finder hint.

articles.title: This Week in Compute Settlement: The Gap Between Shipping and Solving
articles.excerpt: The agent economy doesn't wait for perfect infrastructure. This week showed exactly what that means. Three major infrastructure events happened in parallel. Each solved a different layer of the comput…
articles.body: The agent economy doesn't wait for perfect infrastructure. This week showed exactly what that means. Three major infrastructure events happened in parallel. Each solved a different layer of the compute settlement stack. Each left a different layer unsolved. Put together, they reveal what the market still needs to build. Layer 1: Routing (Solved) IETF published AGTP-COMMERCE as an Internet-Draft in June 2026. It defined the protocol: what gets exchanged in an agent-to-agent transaction, how agents authorize it, what metadata travels with it. Not "who pays" — just "what's the message shape." This week, Nevermined and x402 Foundation both confirmed their routing layers work. Nevermined routes discovery requests. x402 routes micropayments as HTTP headers.

articles.body: Claude Code talks to its backend in the Anthropic Messages format. Any endpoint that accepts that format can stand in for Anthropic's API, which means you can run the same agent loop on DeepSeek, GLM, Qwen or Kimi without a proxy or a converter. I tested this on Claude Code 2.1.284 by asking it to create and write a real file with each model, and re-ran the DeepSeek case on 2.1.296 today. Here is the setup and what I found. Disclosure: I run XHuoAPI, the gateway used below. The same two variables work with any Anthropic-compatible endpoint. Setup Install Claude Code (Node.js 18+): npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code Point it at the gateway.

articles.title: How I let Claude Code handle my accessibility compliance
articles.excerpt: When I started building WebAbility.io, I leaned heavily on Claude Code to move things fast. It could whip up a form, a modal, or even an entire checkout flow in a fraction of the time it would take me…
articles.body: When I started building WebAbility.io, I leaned heavily on Claude Code to move things fast. It could whip up a form, a modal, or even an entire checkout flow in a fraction of the time it would take me. But speed came with a catch: the pages looked fine, but users with screen readers or low vision still hit roadblocks. I noticed missing form labels and low-contrast buttons slipping through. That’s where the WebAbility MCP comes in. I built it to give my coding agent an extra set of eyes: it scans the rendered page against WCAG 2.2 AA, generates accessibility fixes, and then verifies that those fixes actually work. In this post, I’ll walk through how to set up the MCP server with your coding agent and show you the scan-fix-verify loop in action.
articles.author: Sidharth Nayyar

articles.title: TouchGrass AI: Turn Screen Time into Outdoor Adventures
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass 🌿 TouchGrass AI — Less scrolling. More exploring. We spend a significant amount of time looking at screens, oft…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built 🌿 TouchGrass AI — Less scrolling. More exploring. We spend a significant amount of time looking at screens, often struggling to decide how to take a meaningful break. I wanted to build something that uses AI not to keep people glued to their screens, but to encourage them to step away from them. TouchGrass AI is an AI-powered outdoor adventure companion that generates personalized outdoor quests based on four inputs: Activity: Walking, running, nature observation, or gardening. Available time: 10, 20, or 30 minutes. Energy level: Relaxed, moderate, or energetic. Environment: Park, garden, neighbourhood, or trail.

articles.body: 4 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) A KREPE-3 capsule floats inside the Northrup Grumman Cygnus XL 24 cargo spacecraft on October 7. Inside the capsule is a 3-D printed heat shield designed by researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. NASA NASA is testing heat shields that can keep astronauts safe as they return from missions to the Moon and Mars in an unusual way: by taking out the trash. When Northrop Grumman 24 th cargo resupply mission for NASA undocked from the International Space Station, it carried a fleet of 12 small, experimental capsules designed to test the next generation of thermal protection materials that could serve as the foundation for future heat shields.
